Regulatory Transformation

Regulatory Transformation: navigating emerging risks, driving AI adoption and reducing regulatory burden

Regulators are facing a shifting operating environment as technology, markets, environmental pressures and societal expectations evolve faster than traditional regulatory frameworks. Fragmented data and limited intelligence continue to make risk prioritisation difficult.

There is a growing opportunity to use advanced analytics to better target regulatory effort. Many regulators are still working to integrate data across systems, uplift analytical capability and embed insights into everyday decision-making.

AI adoption is also becoming a core regulatory transformation issue. Regulators are seeking to balance opportunities for automation and improved risk identification with the need to manage governance, transparency, bias, legal risk, privacy and public confidence.

At the same time, governments are under pressure to reduce red tape, make faster decisions and manage fiscal constraints. This is driving interest in regulatory consolidation, shared-service models and more consistent approaches to regulatory delivery, while maintaining fairness and strong outcomes.

Regulation Hub Intelligence Brief

AI Brief 318 articles across 8 categories

Aviation safety governance is under simultaneous institutional pressure this fortnight: two ATSB preliminary reports into Sydney Airport taxiing conflicts have put Airservices Australia's safety management systems on the public record, CASA is running a post-implementation fatigue framework review across commercial operators, and the Vietjet financial viability probe signals CASA is prepared to use its economic-fit powers against an international carrier — each thread creating a distinct assurance and capability advisory entry point. The autonomous vehicle legislative window is the fortnight's most time-sensitive opportunity: Tesla's Senate submission to compress Australia's AV framework by two years, backed by a proposed 2027 trial, means the policy design and regulatory-readiness work must begin before the bill drafts lock — state road agencies and the National Transport Commission are the immediate client targets. The ACT Government's $210m Acusensus traffic enforcement contract establishes a replicable outsourced-enforcement-technology model that NSW, Victoria, and Queensland will watch closely, and KPMG's procurement advisory and benefits realisation capability should be positioned before other jurisdictions commence their own procurement processes. AMSA's inaugural National Maritime Stakeholder Forum is a tier-one BD signal — the regulator is deliberately structuring its industry relationship for the first time, and absence from that room is a missed positioning opportunity across port authorities, domestic commercial vessel operators, and maritime safety bodies. The Bus Industry Confederation's post-Greta national bus safety reform campaign is building toward legislative momentum, and KPMG's transport safety bench should be briefing state transport department clients on reform governance implications now. BD concentration this fortnight: AV policy design, CASA-adjacent assurance, and the AMSA forum as the maritime gateway.

Cross-category themes

Regulators across every sector are simultaneously tightening enforcement intensity and expanding personal liability, with AUSTRAC, ASIC, and sector-specific bodies all escalating penalties, issuing new guidance, and signalling Tranche 2-style pressure on previously lower-scrutiny cohorts. The consistent advisory opportunity is compliance uplift and governance readiness, particularly where reform cycles are compressing, AML/CTF for professional services, audit quality for boards, and structural funding changes for education providers.

Implications for KPMGBrief the aged care partner this week on the Ombudsman's Single Assessment System inquiry — any provider or department contact is live pursuit territory for implementation assurance. Pair this with the new ACQSC complaints data release to frame a provider-side governance diagnostic offering before the next reporting cycle.

Financial Services

AI Brief50 articles

ASIC's 2025-26 financial reporting and audit surveillance (REP 842) confirms a sustained quality decline across ASX-listed entities, creating an immediate assurance advisory pull-through for KPMG teams embedded with listed financial services clients. Concurrently, ASIC is consulting on revised financial resources requirements for market operators, a structural regulatory change that will require capital modelling and compliance uplift work across exchange and clearing participants. The Falcon Capital/First Guardian litigation and the Youpla Group director liability findings signal continued ASIC appetite for enforcement against governance failures in wealth and funeral insurance segments, surfacing risk and governance review demand. Australia's APAC-leading data breach fine regime, combined with the ASIC-AFCA scams prevention guidance update, reinforces a compliance technology and controls advisory opportunity across the retail banking and payments client roster.

Implications for KPMGBrief the financial services audit and risk partners on REP 842 before month-end — the surveillance findings give a direct entry point to listed-entity CFOs and audit committees on remediation readiness. Assign a regulatory advisory resource to track the ASIC financial resources consultation closely and position KPMG for submission support and gap analysis work with market operator clients.

Queensland

AI Brief32 articles

Queensland's legislative agenda is active across multiple sectors: mining approval reforms (reducing duplication and refining objection rights) and labour law amendments granting the Deputy Premier strike-breaking powers have passed or are progressing through Parliament, alongside first home buyer housing legislation. The CFMEU inquiry is deepening, with a special prosecutor now sought and evidence emerging of workers being left unprotected after reporting union threats on Cross River Rail. Regulatory enforcement is visible across childcare (21 services sanctioned), e-mobility devices (558 seized), and the Queensland Audit Office tabling 17 reports with costs exceeding targets. AML/CTF compliance obligations under the national Tranche 2 expansion are creating immediate advisory demand for Queensland law firms and professional services.

South Australia

AI Brief29 articles

SafeWork SA is the dominant regulatory force in the current cycle, with multiple active prosecution actions covering asbestos exposure failures at demolition sites, a construction apprentice head injury, and an amusement hire company, signalling sustained enforcement across high-risk industries. Two significant compliance obligations are incoming: SafeWork SA is flagging new psychosocial rules targeting workplace stress and bullying (placing personal liability squarely on employers), and updated Workplace Exposure Limits are being introduced, requiring businesses to audit chemical exposure controls. On the licensing reform front, Retail Drinks Australia is actively challenging SA's alcohol delivery reforms, creating a live advisory opportunity around liquor licensing compliance and industry transition planning. Phosphine regulation changes have been delayed following consultation, offering a window for affected agribusiness clients to engage before rules are finalised.

Tech & AI

Australian public-sector clients are accelerating AI and automation investment while regulators and oversight bodies are simultaneously hardening scrutiny of algorithmic decision-making. The Commonwealth Ombudsman's damning finding on aged care automation — framing the government's tool as a 'technological black box' and drawing explicit parallels to robodebt — signals that every agency deploying automated decisions now faces a live compliance and reputational risk that boards are not yet managing. WA Police conducted 1.38 million facial-recognition scans in a trial with no published governance framework, and the ACT government has committed up to $210 million to AI-powered traffic enforcement via Acusensus, both confirming that enforcement clients are moving faster than their assurance posture. The ATO is mid-refresh on its digital services stack and NDIS is executing a full identity infrastructure migration from PRODA to myID and RAM, both representing active change programmes where advisory and assurance uplift is under-provisioned. At the federal level, a $29.9 million commitment to Australian AI rules signals a policy-implementation gap that will require agency-side capability building. Data centre regulation is crystallising in Victoria and NSW simultaneously, creating regulatory-readiness demand for infrastructure-adjacent clients. Across Defence, Ghost Shark and Bluebottle disclosures confirm autonomous-systems procurement is live and accelerating, with Lightfish adding a naval-permit milestone.

    The AER has finalised tariff structure amendments for Ergon Energy and Energex under the 2025-30 regulatory period and refreshed its Better Resets Handbook, tightening the evidentiary and governance standards networks must meet to justify capex and opex proposals. This signals AER is raising the assurance bar on reset submissions, creating direct demand for independent review, benchmarking, and risk-framework advisory ahead of the next determination cycle.

    Implications: Brief the energy regulation partner this fortnight on positioning KPMG's regulatory assurance and cost-of-service benchmarking capability to Queensland distribution networks facing heightened AER scrutiny on their 2025-30 tariff and reset submissions.

  • Commonwealth Ombudsman commonwealth

    The Commonwealth Ombudsman has concluded a formal inquiry into the Single Assessment System for aged care, finding systemic flaws in automated decision-making including poor explainability, inadequate human oversight, and framework gaps that leave clients exposed to opaque adverse decisions. This signals active regulatory pressure on aged care operators and government agencies to remediate AI governance and algorithmic accountability controls — precisely where KPMG's risk and assurance capability commands premium fees.

    Implications: Brief the Health and Ageing sector partner this fortnight on pursuing the Commonwealth Ombudsman's recommendations as a mandate for an algorithmic accountability and AI governance review engagement across aged care regulatees and the Department itself.

Showing 0 regulators

State-gov priorities

Cited strategic priorities across all 9 jurisdictions, refreshed bi-annually. Every source URL is .gov.au.

Housing supply is the single most universal commitment across jurisdictions, with every state and territory carrying a named target or strategy, ranging from Tasmania's 10,000 affordable homes by 2032 to Victoria's 2.24 million by 2051 and Queensland's one million by 2046; the breadth and ambition of these targets, combined with consistent delivery gaps, creates sustained demand for program assurance, delivery governance, and market-capacity modelling. A second near-universal pattern is domestic industrial policy: the Commonwealth's Future Made in Australia package is mirrored by Made in WA, the SA State Prosperity Project, NSW's reshoring agenda, and Queensland's 30-year resources plan, all centring on sovereign capability, critical minerals, and green manufacturing, with KPMG well-placed on investment-readiness frameworks and industry-development strategy. The energy transition is mainstream in SA, Tasmania, ACT, and the Commonwealth but sits in deliberate tension with NT's and Queensland's resource-sector growth strategies, a divergence that will require jurisdictional stakeholder engagement rather than a single national narrative. Defence is a concentrated but high-value cluster: the Commonwealth's $330 billion integrated investment program, WA's 15-year Defence West strategy, and NT's defence budget priority together represent a sovereign-capability corridor where industry readiness, workforce pipeline, and supply-chain assurance work is still underdeveloped. Crime and public safety reform divides sharply along political lines, with NT and Queensland pursuing punitive youth-justice and crime-reduction agendas while Victoria advances Treaty and mental-health system reform and the ACT embeds a wellbeing budget framework, suggesting two distinct advisory tracks rather than one. Health system reform — aged care transition, hospital safe-staffing, and long-term healthcare planning — appears in the Commonwealth, NSW, SA, and Tasmania, with implementation complexity high enough that program design, workforce modelling, and change assurance represent credible near-term BD entries. Across infrastructure, SA, WA, and the ACT each carry formal 20-year or multi-year strategy documents, while NSW and Queensland are mid-delivery on major transport programs, pointing to infrastructure-pipeline management, benefits realisation, and procurement advisory as durable service lines rather than one-off engagements.

Last refreshed 2026-10-22. Bi-annual schedule; source URLs verified to .gov.au.

Commonwealth
